objective: Architecture patterns: in-cluster versus external reconcilers, hub-and-spoke for many clusters, and state store management (monorepo, repo per team or environment)
secondaryObjectives: Select patterns for a given scenario and explain the trade-offs between them
Pull versus event-driven: scheduled reconciliation versus webhook-triggered reconciliation, and their trade-offs for latency and robustness
Deployment and release patterns: environment promotion through branches or directories, release by pull request, and tagging and pinning versions

The company, the clusters, the teams and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the platform architect at Brightwell Grocers, a fictional supermarket chain. It is moving 40 in-store edge clusters and three regional clusters to GitOps. Store links drop for hours at a time. Sixty development teams will deliver to the fleet.
handover: The draft design: one central reconciler in the head office pushing to all 43 clusters, one repository with a branch per environment.
The review board decides the pattern for the whole fleet.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each design review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: a price-label fix reaches only the 27 stores whose links were up; 13 stores print wrong prices for a weekend.
Week 3: a security fix cherry-picked to staging is missed for prod; prod runs the vulnerable version for three weeks.
Week 4: webhooks sent during a link outage are lost; 9 stores never apply a tax-rate change until someone notices at the tills.

wherePrompt.title: Central hub or an agent per store?
wherePrompt.context: A hub-and-spoke reconciler is simple to run but needs each cluster's credentials and a live link. An in-cluster agent per store needs only read access to Git.

choices.label: Run an in-cluster reconciler in each store cluster pulling from Git; use hub-and-spoke only for the three regional clusters on reliable links

effects.log: Agents per store; a hub for the regions.

choices.feedback: In-cluster agents keep reconciling through link outages and need no inbound credentials; a hub suits a few reliably connected clusters.

choices.label: Keep the central hub for all 43 clusters and accept the gaps
choices.feedback: Simple to operate, but stores drift for every hour their link is down, and the hub holds every cluster's credentials.

choices.label: Have CI push to each store with kubectl when its link is up
choices.feedback: That is not GitOps: nothing reconciles, and stores that missed a push stay on old versions.

layoutPrompt.title: Branches per environment or directories?
layoutPrompt.context: Sixty teams; three environments; staging and prod already differ by 14 unexplained commits.

choices.label: One trunk with a directory per environment (overlays), a repository per team for its apps plus a platform repository; promote by pull request with pinned versions

effects.log: Directories per environment; promotion by pull request.

choices.feedback: Directories on one branch make the difference between environments visible in one diff; per-team repositories match ownership.

choices.label: A single monorepo for all 60 teams with directories per environment and CODEOWNERS
choices.feedback: Promotion is visible, but 60 teams in one repository means noisy reviews and broad write access.

choices.label: Keep a branch per environment and cherry-pick fixes forward
choices.feedback: Cherry-picks drift: what is in prod can no longer be read from one place.

triggerPrompt.title: Polling or webhooks?
triggerPrompt.context: Teams want changes live within a minute. The reconcilers poll Git every 3 minutes by default; webhooks can trigger them at once.

choices.label: Use webhooks to trigger reconciliation at once, and keep periodic polling as the fallback for missed webhooks
choices.feedback: Event-driven for latency, scheduled for robustness: a missed webhook is caught on the next poll.

choices.label: Polling only, every 3 minutes
choices.feedback: Robust but slow; the one-minute target is missed.

choices.label: Webhooks only, with polling turned off to save API calls
choices.feedback: A webhook lost during a store's outage is never retried; that store never reconciles the change.

reflection.question: Write the pattern decision for the fleet: which patterns you chose for reconciler placement, repository layout and triggers, and the trade-off of each.

parts.label: Placement and layout
parts.criteria: In-cluster agents for unreliable stores, a hub for the regions; directories per environment and team repositories with promotion by pull request.
parts.modelAnswer: Stores lose links often, so each runs its own reconciler; the three regions share a hub. One trunk with environment directories and per-team repositories; promotion is a pull request.

parts.label: Triggers
parts.criteria: Webhooks for latency with polling as the fallback.
parts.modelAnswer: Webhooks trigger reconciliation at once; polling every few minutes catches what a webhook misses.

expertPath.text: Read the network report and the draft repository layout first.
Put an in-cluster reconciler in each store; keep hub-and-spoke for the regions.

whereHarm.headline: Reconcile at the edge
whereHarm.body: An in-cluster agent pulls and reconciles whenever the link allows; a push only reaches who is reachable.

layoutHarm.headline: Promote, don't cherry-pick
layoutHarm.body: Environment directories and promotion by pull request keep what differs visible.

triggerHarm.headline: Events for speed, polling for safety
triggerHarm.body: Keep scheduled reconciliation as the fallback for event-driven triggers.

scoring.modelReasoning: Reconciler placement follows connectivity and trust: an in-cluster agent pulls and reconciles whenever it can reach Git and needs no inbound credentials, while a hub-and-spoke reconciler is simpler for a few reliably connected clusters but holds every cluster's credentials. Store desired state so promotion is visible: environment directories (overlays) on one trunk, per-team repositories for ownership, promotion by pull request; branches per environment drift through cherry-picks. Webhooks cut latency, and polling remains the fallback when events are lost.
